title: Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026: Fully Funded Opportunity to Attend COP31 in Türkiye.
summary: The Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) , with funding from the Caribbean Development Bank , has opened applications for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship , an opportunity designed to support emerging Caribbean professionals working or interested in climate change, sustainable development and public engagement. The fellowship will give two young Caribbean professionals the opportunity to attend UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as part of the CCCCC delegation. Selected fellows will receive funding covering return travel, accommodation and a daily per diem, while also receiving official observer access to the COP31 Blue Zone. Beyond attending an international climate conference, the fellowship is structured as a regional capacity-building experience. Fellows will participate in activities before, during and after COP31, gaining exposure to international climate negotiations, regional climate priorities and professional networks that can be used to strengthen climate action across the Caribbean. Application deadline: 21 August 2026. Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026 at a Glance Opportunity Details Fellowship Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship Organiser Caribbean Community Climate Change Centre (CCCCC) Funding partner Caribbean Development Bank Conference UNFCCC COP31 Location Antalya, Türkiye COP31 dates 9–20 November 2026 Number of fellows 2 Age requirement 18–30 Eligibility Nationals of CARICOM Member States Funding Fully funded Travel Return economy airfare Accommodation Hotel accommodation Living support Daily per diem COP access Blue Zone observer accreditation Application deadline 21 August 2026 What Is the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship? The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship is a professional development initiative created to help develop the next generation of Caribbean climate professionals. The programme recognises that international climate negotiations can have significant consequences for Caribbean countries, particularly Small Island Developing States that face challenges related to climate adaptation, climate finance, loss and damage and the Global Goal on Adaptation. Through participation in COP31, fellows will have the opportunity to gain first-hand exposure to the international climate policy process while learning about the role of the CCCCC in coordinating regional climate action. The fellowship is therefore not simply an opportunity to attend COP31. It is designed to help participants understand, contribute to and communicate the climate agenda affecting the Caribbean. Why COP31 Matters to the Caribbean COP31 will bring together governments, climate experts, development partners, advocates and other stakeholders from around the world to discuss international climate action. For Caribbean countries, international climate negotiations are particularly important because climate-related decisions can directly influence the region s ability to respond to climate risks. Among the issues particularly relevant to Caribbean countries are: Climate adaptation Climate finance Loss and damage The Global Goal on Adaptation Sustainable development Climate resilience International cooperation Support for Small Island Developing States The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship aims to equip young professionals with the knowledge and experience needed to understand these discussions and contribute to the region s climate agenda. What Will Fellows Experience? Selected fellows will participate in the full fellowship cycle, beginning before COP31 and continuing after the conference. The programme has three broad stages: 1. Pre-COP Preparation Before travelling to Türkiye, fellows will participate in preparation activities designed to help them understand their role and maximise their contribution to COP31. This preparation can include: Professional development Understanding the UNFCCC process Defining the fellow s role during COP31 Preparing for participation in the CCCCC delegation Understanding Caribbean climate priorities Preparing for knowledge-sharing activities This preparation is intended to ensure that fellows arrive at COP31 ready to participate meaningfully rather than simply attend the conference. 2. Participation During COP31 Fellows will join the CCCCC delegation during COP31 in Antalya. They will have access to the official Blue Zone as observers through the CCCCC delegation quota . This provides an opportunity to experience an important part of the international climate process and attend activities accessible to observers. Fellows may be able to participate in: Plenary sessions Observer-accessible sessions Side events Activities at the CARICOM Pavilion Other relevant COP31 activities 3. Post-COP Knowledge Transfer The fellowship does not end when COP31 concludes. Participants will be expected to contribute to post-conference knowledge-sharing activities across the Caribbean. This means fellows will have an opportunity to take the knowledge, insights and connections developed during COP31 and share them with their organisations, communities and wider Caribbean audiences. What Does the Fellowship Cover? The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship is described as fully funded . The funding package includes several major costs associated with participating in COP31. Return Airfare Selected fellows will receive economy-class return airfare from their home country to Antalya, Türkiye . This removes one of the biggest financial barriers associated with international conference participation. Accommodation The fellowship provides hotel accommodation throughout the conference period . Fellows therefore do not need to independently finance their conference-period accommodation. Daily Per Diem Participants will receive a daily allowance to cover meals and incidental expenses during the fellowship. This provides additional financial support while fellows are participating in COP31. Blue Zone Observer Accreditation Selected fellows will receive official Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation quota . This is an important component of the opportunity because it provides access to COP31 activities available to accredited observers. Mentorship Fellows will receive guidance from experienced members of the CCCCC delegation. Mentorship will take place: Before COP31 During COP31 After COP31 This can help participants better understand the international climate process and make the most of their experience. Professional Development The fellowship also includes structured professional development through: Pre-COP preparation Role definition COP31 participation Post-conference knowledge-sharing Exposure to experienced climate professionals Regional and international networking Who Can Apply for the Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship? The fellowship is specifically designed for young Caribbean professionals between 18 and 30 years old . Applicants should be early-career, mid-career or emerging professionals with a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development . However, applicants must meet several specific eligibility requirements. 1. Age Requirement Applicants must be between 18 and 30 years old . This makes the fellowship particularly relevant to young professionals and emerging leaders who are beginning to establish careers in climate action, development, communications, public engagement or related areas. 2. Citizenship Requirement Applicants must be nationals of a CARICOM Member State . This is a key eligibility condition. The fellowship is specifically designed to strengthen Caribbean climate leadership, meaning applicants from countries outside the CARICOM membership framework do not qualify simply because they work on climate-related issues. 3. Caribbean-Based Organisation Affiliation Applicants must be affiliated with or work with a Caribbean-based organisation . The organisation may fall into a number of categories, including: Youth organisations Non-governmental organisations Community-based organisations Private-sector organisations Public-sector institutions Other organisations working in climate, development or public engagement 4. Education, Employment or Organisational Involvement Applicants should currently be: Enrolled in tertiary education; Employed; or Actively involved with a relevant organisation. Their work, studies or involvement should connect to climate change, development, public engagement or related areas. 5. Climate and Sustainable Development Interest Applicants should demonstrate a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development . The programme is intended for people who can contribute to the Caribbean s climate agenda and eventually help translate international climate discussions into meaningful regional action. 6. Cannot Be an Official Party Negotiator Applicants must not currently be serving as an official Party negotiator . The fellowship is aimed at emerging professionals who will participate through the CCCCC delegation rather than individuals already serving as official government negotiators in the UNFCCC process. What Organisations Can Applicants Come From? The fellowship is open to individuals connected to a range of organisations. Potential applicants may be affiliated with: Youth Organisations Young people involved in youth-led initiatives and organisations can apply if they meet the other requirements. Non-Governmental Organisations Professionals and emerging leaders working with NGOs on climate, development, advocacy or related issues may be eligible. Community-Based Organisations Applicants involved in community-level climate or development initiatives may also qualify. Private-Sector Organisations Young professionals working in businesses or other private-sector organisations can apply where their work or interests align with the fellowship requirements. Public-Sector Institutions Applicants working in government or public institutions can also be eligible, provided they meet the requirements and are not serving as official Party negotiators. Other Relevant Organisations The fellowship also recognises organisations working in areas such as: Climate action Sustainable development Public engagement Environmental issues Community development Related areas of regional importance The Blue Zone Access Explained One of the most valuable features of the fellowship is access to the COP31 Blue Zone . Selected fellows will receive observer accreditation through the CCCCC s available quota. This means fellows who are selected can attend activities accessible to accredited observers, including relevant plenaries, sessions, side events and activities at the CARICOM Pavilion. The fellowship also encourages participants to explore accreditation through their respective national delegations. National delegation accreditation could potentially provide additional opportunities to observe negotiation processes and contribute to country delegations where appropriate. However, this additional accreditation is not guaranteed . The decision to provide accreditation through a national government rests entirely with the relevant government. The CCCCC may provide a supporting letter to the appropriate government upon request, but this does not guarantee national delegation accreditation. Importantly, a fellow who does not receive national delegation accreditation can still participate through their Blue Zone observer accreditation provided via the CCCCC delegation . Application Requirements Applicants need to prepare several important materials before applying. 1. Current Curriculum Vitae Applicants must provide a current CV. The CV should clearly demonstrate relevant aspects of the applicant s background, including: Education Professional experience Volunteer involvement Climate-related work Relevant skills Organisational involvement Applicants should make sure their CV clearly communicates their connection to climate action, sustainable development, public engagement or other relevant areas. APPLY HERE. 2. Written Application of 1,200–1,500 Words Applicants must submit a written application between 1,200 and 1,500 words . The application must address three major areas. Professional Development Applicants should explain how participation in the fellowship would contribute to their professional development. This section should address: Skills they expect to develop Knowledge they hope to gain Experience they want to acquire Their career trajectory Why this is the right time for them to participate Applicants should demonstrate that they have thought carefully about how the fellowship fits into their professional journey. Institutional Impact Applicants should explain how their participation would benefit their organisation or institution. They should provide a realistic plan explaining how they intend to share: Knowledge Insights Lessons from COP31 Professional networks Relevant climate information with their colleagues, organisation or community. A strong answer should demonstrate that the benefits of the fellowship will extend beyond the individual participant. Caribbean Climate Literacy Applicants must explain how their COP31 experience will help translate complex climate discussions into accessible information for Caribbean audiences. The goal is to demonstrate how the applicant can contribute to stronger climate literacy and public engagement across the Caribbean . A short supporting statement from the applicant s organisation or institution is encouraged. How Will Applications Be Assessed? Applications will primarily be assessed according to the strength, clarity and credibility of the three required written statements. The selection panel will give particular consideration to several factors. Commitment to the Caribbean Climate Agenda Applicants should demonstrate genuine interest in the climate issues affecting Caribbean countries and the wider region. Professional Value The selection panel will consider how valuable the fellowship would be to the applicant s professional development. Applicants should therefore explain why participation at this particular stage of their career would make a meaningful difference. Institutional Knowledge Transfer Applicants need to present a credible plan for transferring the knowledge and insights gained through COP31 to their organisation or community. Climate Literacy Contribution The panel will assess how effectively applicants can help make climate discussions understandable and accessible to Caribbean communities. Communication Skills Applicants should demonstrate an ability to communicate climate information effectively. This is particularly important because fellows are expected to help translate international climate discussions into accessible information. Potential Impact Beyond COP31 The selection process will also consider whether the fellowship could produce meaningful impact after the conference. The ideal candidate will not simply benefit personally from attending COP31 but will use the experience to contribute to wider Caribbean climate action. Interview and Final Selection After applications have been reviewed, shortlisted candidates will be invited to an interview with a CCCCC selection panel . Following the selection process, only two fellows will be selected. Because there are only two fellowship positions, applicants should ensure that their application clearly communicates their motivation, experience, potential impact and connection to the Caribbean climate agenda. For more information VISIT HERE. Important Dates Applicants should take note of the following dates: Applications open: 10 August 2026 Application deadline: 21 August 2026 COP31: 9–20 November 2026 Location: Antalya, Türkiye Only a short period is available between the opening of applications and the deadline, so eligible applicants should begin preparing their CV and written application as early as possible. How to Prepare a Strong Application Applicants can take several steps to make their application more compelling. Research Caribbean Climate Priorities Develop a clear understanding of the climate challenges facing Caribbean countries and the importance of issues such as adaptation, climate finance, loss and damage and climate resilience. Connect COP31 to Your Career Do not simply state that attending COP31 would be valuable. Explain exactly how the experience would support your professional goals and the skills you want to develop. Present a Realistic Knowledge-Sharing Plan The fellowship places significant emphasis on institutional impact. Think about what you would actually do after COP31 to share your knowledge. For example, you could consider activities such as: Internal presentations Community discussions Educational content Workshops Social media campaigns Articles Youth engagement activities Climate literacy initiatives Demonstrate Communication Ability Since climate literacy is an important part of the fellowship, applicants should demonstrate their ability to communicate complex subjects in ways that ordinary audiences can understand. Show Regional Commitment Explain how your experience, interests or work connects with the needs and priorities of Caribbean communities. Proofread the Written Application The written component has a specific 1,200–1,500-word requirement . Applicants should ensure their submission remains within the required range while answering all three areas fully. Why This Fellowship Is a Valuable Opportunity The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship combines international exposure, professional development, mentorship and practical climate engagement. Selected fellows will have the opportunity to: Attend COP31 in Türkiye. Receive fully funded return economy airfare. Receive accommodation during the conference period. Receive a daily per diem. Obtain Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation. Receive mentorship from experienced climate professionals. Learn more about the UNFCCC process. Develop professional skills. Build international and regional networks. Learn more about Caribbean climate priorities. Participate in COP31-related activities. Share knowledge with organisations and communities after the conference. Contribute to stronger climate literacy across the Caribbean. The fellowship therefore has the potential to benefit both the selected individuals and the wider organisations and communities they represent. A Platform for the Next Generation of Caribbean Climate Leaders Climate change presents significant challenges for Caribbean countries, particularly because many countries in the region are vulnerable to climate impacts despite contributing relatively little to global emissions. Developing professionals who understand international climate negotiations and can communicate climate issues effectively is therefore important for the region s future. The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship seeks to contribute to this effort by giving emerging professionals direct exposure to COP31 while preparing them to take the knowledge gained back to their communities. The programme s emphasis on knowledge transfer is particularly significant. Fellows are expected to help ensure that their experience benefits more than just themselves. Conclusion The Caribbean Climate Leaders Fellowship 2026 offers two young Caribbean professionals the opportunity to experience UNFCCC COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye , while developing professional skills, building networks and contributing to the Caribbean s climate agenda. The fellowship is fully funded, covering return economy airfare, accommodation and a daily per diem. Selected fellows will also receive Blue Zone observer accreditation through the CCCCC delegation and mentorship before, during and after COP31. Applicants must be 18–30 years old, nationals of a CARICOM Member State and affiliated with or working with a Caribbean-based organisation . They should have a strong interest in climate change and sustainable development and must not currently be serving as official Party negotiators. The application requires a current CV and a 1,200–1,500-word written application addressing professional development, institutional impact and Caribbean climate literacy. With only two fellows to be selected, applicants should focus on demonstrating their commitment to the Caribbean climate agenda, their ability to communicate climate information and their potential to create impact beyond COP31. Application deadline: 21 August 2026. For more OFY Fellowship opportunities CLICK HERE. title: LIVES Doctoral Programme 2026–2029: PhD Training Opportunity for Early-Stage Researchers in Europe
summary: The Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES) has opened applications for its next cohort of doctoral researchers, offering early-stage PhD candidates the opportunity to join an internationally oriented and interdisciplinary doctoral programme focused on life course and lifespan research . The LIVES Doctoral Programme is designed for researchers whose doctoral projects examine how people s lives develop and change over time, including issues surrounding education, employment, health, ageing, social transitions, family experiences, public policy, and other factors that influence individual and collective life trajectories. The programme has been running since 2012 and has supported more than 130 PhD graduates . For the upcoming cohort, LIVES is inviting applications from eligible doctoral students who want to strengthen their theoretical knowledge, methodological expertise, interdisciplinary research skills, and academic networks. The new cohort will run from December 2026 to February 2029 , with activities taking place at the University of Geneva and the University of Lausanne in Switzerland . Opportunity Overview The LIVES Doctoral Programme provides structured doctoral training for PhD candidates whose research is connected to the study of life courses and human development across time. Rather than being a conventional PhD scholarship or a standalone doctoral degree, the programme functions as an additional specialised training programme that doctoral candidates can undertake alongside their existing disciplinary PhD training. This makes it particularly valuable for researchers who are already enrolled in doctoral programmes and want to develop stronger expertise in life course theory, longitudinal research, interdisciplinary approaches, and advanced methodological techniques. Key details at a glance Programme: LIVES Doctoral Programme Cohort: December 2026 – February 2029 Host: Swiss Centre of Expertise in Life Course Research (LIVES) Locations: University of Geneva and University of Lausanne, Switzerland Opportunity type: Doctoral training programme Target applicants: Early-stage PhD/doctoral students Research focus: Life course and lifespan research Eligible fields: Social sciences, psychology, health sciences and related disciplines Study/research format: In-person workshops, training sessions and academic events English requirement: Minimum B2 level Application deadline: 30 September 2026 Admissions decision: No later than the end of October 2026 Programme start: December 2026 What Is the LIVES Doctoral Programme? The LIVES Doctoral Programme is a specialised interdisciplinary programme developed to support doctoral researchers studying life course processes. The programme recognises that important outcomes in people s lives are often shaped by events and experiences occurring at different points throughout their lives. Researchers may therefore need approaches that can connect childhood experiences, education, employment, health, family life, ageing, social change and other transitions across time. LIVES brings together doctoral researchers working on these kinds of questions and provides them with opportunities to receive training from specialists, exchange ideas with other PhD candidates and obtain feedback from experienced researchers. The programme also places considerable emphasis on longitudinal methods and life course analysis, making it particularly relevant to researchers working with data that follows people, groups or populations over extended periods. Who Should Apply? The programme is aimed at early-stage doctoral students whose PhD research has a clear life course or lifespan perspective. Potential applicants may be researching a wide variety of topics. What matters most is the connection between the doctoral project and life course research. Applicants may come from disciplines such as: Sociology Demography Psychology Epidemiology Economics Political Science Neuroscience History Gender Studies Health sciences Other related disciplines The programme is interdisciplinary, meaning that applicants do not necessarily need to come from one specific academic department. Examples of Eligible Research Topics LIVES provides several examples of research areas that can fit within its programme. 1. Early-Life Events and Later Outcomes Research may investigate how experiences during childhood, adolescence or other early stages of life affect outcomes later in life. For example, a doctoral researcher could study how childhood socioeconomic circumstances influence educational achievement, employment opportunities, health or social mobility later in adulthood. 2. Life Trajectories Across Different Domains Applicants may study how people s trajectories develop across different areas of life. Possible domains include: Education Employment Health Family Social relationships Economic circumstances Migration Ageing Such research can examine how developments in one area of life interact with developments in another. 3. Turning Points and Transitions Life course research can also focus on major transitions and turning points in individual biographies. Examples could include: Transition from school to work Marriage or partnership Parenthood Retirement Migration Career changes Major health events Educational transitions Researchers may investigate what causes these transitions and how they affect people s subsequent trajectories. 4. Accumulation and Depletion Across the Life Span The programme also welcomes research examining how advantages and disadvantages accumulate or diminish over time. This could involve studying how socioeconomic advantage, educational opportunities, health conditions or social resources build up across different stages of life. 5. Longitudinal Methods and Data Analysis Applicants whose projects involve longitudinal datasets and methods may find the programme particularly relevant. Longitudinal research allows researchers to examine change over time rather than relying solely on observations from a single point. 6. Changing Social Norms Around Age and Ageing Another potential area concerns changing attitudes, expectations and social norms surrounding age and ageing. Researchers could examine how societies understand different stages of life and how these expectations change over generations. 7. Life Course Research and Public Policy The programme also welcomes research examining how life course concepts can contribute to public policy. This could include research into policies affecting education, employment, healthcare, ageing, family life, social protection or other areas of public policy. Programme Structure The LIVES Doctoral Programme is organised over approximately two years and combines theoretical training, methodological workshops, doctoral presentations and individual academic feedback. Participants are expected to attend a number of activities throughout the programme. The structure includes four intensive sessions on theories and concepts in life course research . Each theoretical session lasts approximately two to three days and is designed to strengthen participants understanding of the conceptual foundations of life course research. The programme also provides four methodological workshops focusing on longitudinal and life course analysis. These workshops last approximately two to four days and are intended to develop participants ability to apply appropriate methods to life course research. LIVES Doctoriales A particularly important part of the programme is the LIVES Doctoriales . Two annual Doctoriales are organised during the programme. These provide PhD candidates with an opportunity to present their research to senior scholars and receive expert feedback. Presenting doctoral research in this setting can help researchers identify weaknesses, refine research questions, improve theoretical frameworks and strengthen methodological approaches. It also provides valuable experience in communicating academic research to an expert audience. Individual Expert Feedback Participants also receive an individual feedback session . During this session, doctoral researchers have the opportunity to discuss and exchange ideas about their research with an invited expert. This personalised academic interaction can be particularly useful when a researcher is trying to address a difficult theoretical, methodological or conceptual issue within their thesis. Commitment Required from Participants Applicants should understand that joining the LIVES Doctoral Programme requires an active commitment to participation. Participants are expected to attend at least 13 days of their choice from the eight doctoral workshops . The programme also identifies certain activities as compulsory. According to the call, Session 1 and the two LIVES Doctoriales are compulsory , and selected workshops and Doctoriales must be attended in person . The programme is designed to complement, rather than replace, a participant s existing disciplinary doctoral training. PhD candidates who want to undertake LIVES training alongside their disciplinary training are explicitly welcome. For example, a doctoral researcher may continue specialised training in areas such as social psychology, neuroscience or another discipline while participating in the LIVES programme. Certificates and ECTS Credits Participants can receive certificates of attendance for the programme modules. The certificates include the corresponding number of ECTS credits , providing formal recognition of the training completed through the programme. This can be useful for doctoral researchers who need evidence of additional academic training as part of their doctoral development. Financial Support for Participants The programme provides financial assistance to support participation, although applicants should note that this is not presented as a full doctoral scholarship covering all living and study expenses. Support for Swiss-Based PhD Candidates For PhD candidates based in Switzerland, travel expenses are reimbursed based on the cost of a half-fare second-class ticket . Support for International PhD Candidates International PhD candidates can receive financial assistance for travel of up to CHF 200 per session , for a maximum of five sessions . This means eligible international participants could potentially receive up to CHF 1,000 in travel support across five sessions, subject to the programme s applicable conditions. Accommodation Support LIVES also indicates that accommodation subsidies are available for a limited number of students . International applicants who require accommodation assistance should contact the programme for further information. Applicants from outside Switzerland are specifically asked in the application form whether they wish to request financial assistance for accommodation. Meals and Breaks The programme also provides some meal-related support. During workshops, lunch breaks are covered . During the LIVES Doctoriales, lunch and coffee breaks are covered . Applicants should nevertheless carefully review the programme s financial arrangements and contact LIVES if they require clarification regarding expenses that are not specifically listed as covered. Eligibility Requirements Applicants must satisfy several conditions before applying. 1. Your PhD Must Have a Life Course or Life Span Perspective The doctoral thesis must incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective. This is one of the most important eligibility requirements. Simply being a doctoral student in a social science or health-related field is not enough. The research itself should meaningfully engage with life course or lifespan concepts. 2. Academic Discipline The doctoral research should have a disciplinary background in an eligible or related field. The call specifically mentions: Sociology Demography Psychology Epidemiology Economics Political Science Neuroscience History Gender Studies Related fields may also be considered where the doctoral project has a clear connection to life course research. 3. Existing Academic Affiliation Applicants must already be affiliated with an academic institution. This means the programme is intended for people who are already doctoral candidates rather than individuals who are merely planning to start a PhD in the future. An official document confirming academic affiliation must be submitted with the application. 4. PhD Funding The PhD thesis must be funded for the length of the doctoral programme. Funding can come from: An academic institution; or Third-party funding. Applicants should therefore ensure that their existing doctoral funding arrangement covers the required period. 5. English Language Ability Applicants must be able to speak and write English fluently. The minimum stated level is B2 . Because the programme involves workshops, academic presentations, discussions and written research materials, applicants should be comfortable communicating their research in English. Where Can Applicants Be Based? The programme is open to doctoral students based in Switzerland and Europe . The call does not specify a particular racial, ethnic or nationality restriction. Therefore, eligibility is primarily determined by the applicant s academic status, institutional affiliation, research topic, funding and geographical location rather than race. International applicants outside Switzerland can receive certain travel assistance, subject to the programme s funding conditions. Required Application Documents Applicants must submit several supporting documents alongside the application form. 1. Cover Letter Applicants must provide a cover letter explaining their motivation for joining the LIVES Doctoral Programme. The letter should clearly explain: Why the applicant wants to participate How their PhD research relates to life course research What they hope to gain from the programme How the programme complements their existing doctoral training Why the applicant would contribute meaningfully to the LIVES doctoral community 2. Curriculum Vitae A CV must be submitted. The CV should clearly present the applicant s academic background, research experience, publications where applicable, professional experience, methodological skills, conferences and other relevant achievements. 3. PhD Project Title and Abstract Applicants must provide the title and an abstract of their PhD project , with the abstract being approximately 500 words maximum . This section should clearly communicate the research question, objectives, theoretical approach, methodology and relevance of the research to life course or lifespan studies. 4. Supervisor Recommendation Letter Applicants must submit a one-page letter of support from their PhD supervisor or supervisors . The recommendation should demonstrate the supervisor s support for the applicant s participation and establish the relevance of the LIVES programme to the doctoral research. 5. Official Academic Affiliation Document Applicants must provide an official document certifying their affiliation with an academic institution. This is important because applicants must already be affiliated with an academic institution to qualify. Application Form Information The online application form requests several pieces of information from candidates. Applicants should be prepared to provide: First name Last name Institutional email Postal address City Postal code Country Academic institution Discipline Source of PhD funding Name of PhD supervisor Supervisor s email address Applicants must also upload their supporting documents. The system allows up to 10 files , with a maximum total file size of 50 MB . Accepted file formats include: TXT RTF PDF DOC DOCX ODT PPT PPTX ODP XLS XLSX ODS After uploading the documents, applicants are instructed to check the boxes corresponding to the documents that should be submitted with their application. Accommodation Assistance for International Applicants Applicants from outside Switzerland will be asked whether they want to request financial assistance for accommodation. The form provides two options: Yes No Applicants who require accommodation assistance should indicate this during the application process and may also contact the programme for additional information about eligibility and available subsidies. Application Deadline The deadline to apply for the LIVES Doctoral Programme is: 30 September 2026 Applicants should avoid waiting until the final day to submit their materials. Because the application requires multiple supporting documents, including a supervisor recommendation letter and official proof of academic affiliation, candidates should begin preparing their applications well before the deadline. What Happens After Applying? The admissions process is expected to be completed relatively soon after the deadline. According to LIVES, admission decisions will be confirmed no later than the end of October 2026 . The new cohort is scheduled to begin in December 2026 . Successful applicants will subsequently sign an agreement involving: The PhD candidate Their supervisor or supervisors The LIVES Doctoral Programme This agreement formalises participation in the programme. Why This Programme Could Be Valuable for PhD Researchers The LIVES Doctoral Programme offers several potential academic and professional advantages. Interdisciplinary Training Life course research often crosses disciplinary boundaries. The programme brings together researchers from different academic backgrounds, allowing participants to encounter theories and methods beyond their primary discipline. Advanced Methodological Skills The methodological workshops focus on longitudinal and life course analysis, which can strengthen a researcher s ability to analyse changes and developments over time. Expert Academic Feedback Participants have opportunities to present their research to senior scholars and receive specialised feedback. This can be extremely valuable during the early stages of a PhD, when research questions, theoretical frameworks and methodologies are still being refined. International Academic Network The programme creates a community of international PhD researchers working on related questions. Building relationships with other doctoral researchers can lead to future collaborations, research exchanges, conference opportunities and broader academic networks. Exposure to Leading Life Course Research Participants can deepen their understanding of life course theories, concepts and research methods through structured sessions and workshops. Formal Recognition Certificates and ECTS credits provide formal recognition of participation in the programme s training modules. Important Considerations Before Applying Applicants should carefully assess whether the programme fits their current doctoral situation. First, this is not an opportunity for someone who has not yet started a PhD . The applicant must already be affiliated with an academic institution. Second, the PhD must be funded for the duration of the programme. Third, the research must genuinely incorporate a life course or lifespan perspective. Applicants should therefore avoid presenting a project that only has a superficial connection to the topic. Fourth, participation involves in-person attendance in Switzerland. Candidates should consider their ability to attend the required sessions and workshops. Finally, applicants should not assume that the travel assistance represents complete financial coverage. The call specifies particular limits for travel and indicates that accommodation subsidies are available only to a limited number of students. How to Prepare a Strong Application A competitive application should demonstrate a clear connection between the applicant s doctoral research and the objectives of the LIVES programme. Make the Life Course Connection Explicit Do not assume that the selection committee will automatically see the connection. Explain precisely how the thesis examines: Change over time Life transitions Trajectories Turning points Accumulation or depletion Age and ageing Intergenerational processes Longitudinal patterns Policy implications across the life span Strengthen the Motivation Letter The cover letter should go beyond saying that the programme is prestigious or interesting. Explain specifically why LIVES is relevant to the doctoral project and identify the theoretical or methodological skills you hope to develop. Prepare the Supervisor Early Because a supervisor support letter is required, applicants should approach their supervisor well before the deadline. Waiting until the final days could create unnecessary delays. Make the 500-Word Abstract Count The abstract has a maximum of approximately 500 words, so every paragraph should have a purpose. A strong abstract should quickly establish the research problem, research question, theoretical perspective, methodology and expected contribution. title: Horizon Europe and EU Research Funding 2026: Explore European Commission Research, Innovation, Climate, Health and Regional Development Funding Opportunities
summary: The European Union provides extensive funding opportunities for research, innovation, healthcare, climate action, regional development, sustainability, and economic growth through a range of major programmes managed or supported by the European Commission . Among these programmes, Horizon Europe stands out as the European Union s principal research and innovation programme for the 2021–2027 period, with a substantial budget of €95.5 billion . The programme is designed to support cutting-edge research and innovation, strengthen European competitiveness, address global challenges, contribute to the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, and help develop technologies and knowledge capable of creating long-term social and economic impact. However, Horizon Europe is only one component of the wider European funding landscape. The European Commission also highlights programmes covering healthcare, climate change, biodiversity, clean energy, regional development, economic and social cohesion, technical reforms, agriculture, maritime development, and research in strategic industrial sectors such as coal and steel. This makes the European Commission s research and innovation funding ecosystem particularly relevant to universities, researchers, research organizations, businesses, public institutions, innovators, and organizations working on major societal and economic challenges. What Is Horizon Europe? Horizon Europe is the European Union s research and innovation programme for the period 2021–2027 . With a total budget of €95.5 billion , it represents one of the world s major public funding frameworks for research and innovation. The programme is designed to support projects that can contribute to: Scientific excellence Technological development Innovation Economic growth Industrial competitiveness Climate action Sustainable development Policy development International collaboration Job creation Knowledge creation Technological advancement Horizon Europe also seeks to strengthen the European Research Area by supporting collaboration among researchers, institutions, businesses, policymakers, and other stakeholders. Key Objectives of Horizon Europe The Horizon Europe programme has been established to address both European and global challenges through research and innovation. Its broad objectives include: 1. Tackling Climate Change Research and innovation supported through Horizon Europe can contribute to Europe s climate objectives and broader global efforts to address climate change. Projects can help develop new technologies, processes, policies, and approaches capable of reducing environmental impacts and supporting climate resilience. 2. Supporting the UN Sustainable Development Goals Horizon Europe contributes to efforts aimed at achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) . Research and innovation can help address interconnected challenges involving: Poverty Health Education Energy Climate Food systems Industry Infrastructure Sustainable cities Environmental protection Economic development 3. Strengthening European Competitiveness Innovation is considered an important driver of economic growth. Horizon Europe therefore supports the development and dissemination of knowledge and technologies that can strengthen Europe s industrial competitiveness. 4. Creating Jobs and Economic Growth Research and innovation can create new industries, products, services, technologies, and employment opportunities. The programme seeks to maximize the economic and societal impact of research investments. 5. Strengthening International Collaboration Horizon Europe facilitates collaboration between researchers, institutions, organizations, and other stakeholders. This collaborative approach can help researchers combine expertise, infrastructure, data, and resources to address complex challenges. Why EU Research and Innovation Funding Matters Research and innovation are central to addressing challenges that cannot be solved through isolated actions. Issues such as climate change, public health, energy security, industrial transformation, environmental degradation, and sustainable development require long-term investment in knowledge and technology. European Union funding programmes help support this work by providing financial resources for research, innovation, infrastructure, collaboration, and implementation. For researchers and organizations, these programmes can provide opportunities to transform research ideas into: New technologies Scientific discoveries Innovative products Policy recommendations Demonstration projects Sustainable solutions New businesses Improved public service Apply here Other European Commission Funding Programmes The European Commission s research and innovation funding landscape extends beyond Horizon Europe. The information provided highlights several additional programmes. These include: EU4Health Cohesion Fund LIFE Programme European Regional Development Fund Technical Support Instrument European Structural and Investment Funds Research Fund for Coal and Steel Each programme has a different purpose, target group, funding structure, and eligibility framework. Visit here for more details on Horizon Europe and EU Research Funding 2026 EU4Health Programme The EU4Health programme is the European Union s fourth and largest health programme since the EU health programmes began in 2003. It has a budget of €5.3 billion . The programme is implemented by the European Health and Digital Executive Agency (HaDEA) . EU4Health is designed to strengthen Europe s health systems and contribute to improved preparedness and resilience. The programme is particularly relevant to organizations and stakeholders working on health-related challenges and European health priorities. Why EU4Health Is Important Healthcare systems face increasingly complex challenges, including emerging health threats, cross-border health issues, and the need for stronger preparedness. A large-scale EU health programme can support initiatives that contribute to: Health system resilience Public health Health preparedness European health cooperation Health-related innovation Capacity building Specific eligibility and funding conditions depend on individual EU4Health calls. Cohesion Fund The Cohesion Fund is another major European Union funding instrument. It is specifically aimed at EU countries whose gross national income (GNI) per inhabitant is less than 90% of the EU average . Its overarching objective is to help reduce economic and social disparities between regions and countries within the European Union. The fund also supports sustainable development. Its priorities can therefore contribute to strengthening economic and social cohesion while encouraging environmentally sustainable development. LIFE Programme: Climate, Nature and Clean Energy Funding The LIFE Programme 2021–2027 is another important European Union funding programme highlighted on the European Commission s research and innovation funding page. The programme is divided into four major sub-programmes: Nature and Biodiversity This area focuses on protecting biodiversity and supporting nature conservation. Potential areas include: Biodiversity protection Ecosystem conservation Nature restoration Environmental management Circular Economy and Quality of Life This component addresses environmental challenges associated with resource use, pollution, waste, and sustainable production and consumption. Climate Change Mitigation and Adaptation This area supports efforts to: Reduce greenhouse gas emissions Address climate change Improve climate resilience Develop adaptation strategies Support climate-related innovation Clean Energy Transition The clean energy component supports the transition toward more sustainable energy systems. This can include initiatives designed to improve energy efficiency and accelerate the adoption of clean energy solutions. European Regional Development Fund The European Regional Development Fund (ERDF) aims to strengthen economic and social cohesion within the European Union. A major purpose of the fund is to help correct economic and regional imbalances. The ERDF focuses investment on priority areas that can contribute to regional development. One of its important areas is: Research and innovation. This makes the ERDF particularly relevant to regional initiatives seeking to strengthen innovation ecosystems, economic development, infrastructure, and research capabilities. Technical Support Instrument The Technical Support Instrument provides tailor-made technical expertise to EU countries undertaking reforms. Rather than functioning solely as conventional project funding, the instrument provides technical assistance designed around specific reform needs. This can help participating countries: Design reforms Implement reforms Strengthen administrative capacity Improve institutional performance Develop technical solutions Address complex policy challenges The programme is particularly relevant to public authorities working on structural and institutional reforms. European Structural and Investment Funds The European Structural and Investment Funds (ESIF) represent another major component of European Union funding. According to the information provided, more than half of EU funding is channelled through the five European Structural and Investment Funds. These funds are jointly managed by: The European Commission European Union Member States Their broad purpose is to support: Job creation Sustainable economic development Social development Environmental sustainability Regional development Five European Structural and Investment Funds The five funds cover different areas of European development. They include: 1. European Regional Development Fund Supports regional economic and social development, including research and innovation. 2. European Social Fund Supports employment, skills, education, training, and social inclusion. 3. Cohesion Fund Supports EU countries meeting the relevant income criterion and contributes to economic and social cohesion. 4. European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development Supports rural development and agricultural priorities. 5. European Maritime and Fisheries Fund Supports areas associated with maritime activities, fisheries, and related development priorities. The eligibility and funding mechanisms differ among the individual funds. Research Fund for Coal and Steel The Research Fund for Coal and Steel (RFCS) supports research projects related to the coal and steel sectors. The fund provides support to organizations including: Universities Research centres Private companies According to the information provided, approximately €55 million is made available annually for research in these sectors, with the historical reference noting €47.7 million for 2015. The RFCS provides a mechanism for supporting research and technological development in sectors undergoing significant industrial transformation. Who Can Benefit From European Research and Innovation Funding? Because the page covers multiple funding programmes rather than a single grant competition, the potential beneficiaries vary considerably. Depending on the programme and specific call, funding opportunities may be relevant to: Universities Academic researchers Research centres Scientific institutions Private companies Innovative businesses Public authorities Regional organizations Non-governmental organizations where eligible Healthcare organizations Environmental organizations Agricultural organizations Industrial stakeholders Technology developers International research partnerships However, applicants should not assume that an organization automatically qualifies simply because it belongs to one of these categories. Eligibility must always be checked against the specific funding call. What Types of Projects Can EU Funding Support? The broad funding ecosystem described on the European Commission page covers an extensive range of activities. Depending on the programme, projects can address areas such as: Scientific research Technological innovation Climate change Environmental protection Biodiversity Healthcare Clean energy Circular economy Regional development Sustainable agriculture Rural development Maritime development Industrial research Coal and steel research Economic development Social development Institutional reform This breadth makes EU funding particularly significant for organizations working on complex multidisciplinary challenges. Horizon Europe and International Collaboration One of the central strengths of Horizon Europe is its emphasis on collaboration. Modern research challenges often require expertise from multiple disciplines and institutions. For example, a climate project might require collaboration among: Climate scientists Economists Engineers Policymakers Technology companies Environmental organizations Data scientists Similarly, a healthcare innovation project might require cooperation among: Medical researchers Universities Hospitals Technology developers Public authorities Health organizations Horizon Europe s collaborative structure is designed to facilitate such partnerships and maximize the impact of research and innovation. Contribution to the European Research Area Horizon Europe also contributes to strengthening the European Research Area (ERA) . The European Research Area seeks to create stronger cooperation and coordination across European research systems. By supporting collaboration and knowledge sharing, EU research funding can help: Connect researchers Improve research capacity Share scientific knowledge Encourage innovation Strengthen institutions Improve the impact of research investments Is There a Deadline for This Opportunity? No specific application deadline is stated in the information provided. This is important because the page is a general overview of EU funding programmes and does not represent one individual grant call. Different programmes and individual calls have different: Opening dates Submission deadlines Eligibility rules Funding amounts Application procedures Consortium requirements Applicants should therefore identify the specific programme and call relevant to their project before preparing an application. How to Find an Appropriate EU Funding Opportunity Researchers and organizations interested in EU funding should begin by identifying the nature of their project. Step 1: Define the Project Clearly establish: The problem being addressed Research objectives Expected outcomes Target beneficiaries Proposed methodology Innovation component Expected impact Step 2: Identify the Appropriate Programme A climate project may be more relevant to LIFE or a suitable Horizon Europe call, while a health-focused initiative could be relevant to EU4Health. Regional infrastructure or innovation projects may fall under ERDF or related funding instruments. Step 3: Check Eligibility Review the specific call carefully. Important eligibility considerations can include: Applicant type Country eligibility Consortium requirements Research area Project duration Funding limits Co-financing requirements Partnership requirements Step 4: Review the Deadline Every individual call has its own submission deadline. Applicants should never rely on the general programme period as an application deadline. Step 5: Prepare the Proposal A competitive EU proposal generally needs to clearly demonstrate: Excellence Relevance Innovation Feasibility Impact Appropriate implementation Strong partnership arrangements where required Key Difference Between Horizon Europe and Other EU Funds Although all of these programmes form part of the broader European funding ecosystem, they serve different purposes. For example: Programme Main Focus Horizon Europe Research and innovation EU4Health Health LIFE Environment, climate and clean energy ERDF Regional development and cohesion Cohesion Fund Economic and social cohesion Technical Support Instrument Reform support and technical expertise ESIF Regional, social, agricultural and maritime development RFCS Coal and steel research This distinction is important when searching for funding because selecting an inappropriate programme can result in an application that does not align with the fund s objectives. Why Researchers and Innovators Should Explore EU Funding European Union research and innovation programmes provide access to some of the world s largest public funding mechanisms for research, development, sustainability, and innovation. For eligible organizations, successful funding can provide resources to: Conduct research Develop new technologies Test innovative solutions Build partnerships Address societal challenges Expand research capacity Strengthen institutions Create economic opportunities Support environmental sustainability Contribute to international policy objectives For researchers and organizations working on ambitious projects, EU funding can therefore provide an important route for moving ideas from research and development toward real-world implementation. Important Considerations Before Applying Potential applicants should remember that the information on this page is a programme overview, not a single funding application announcement . Before applying, applicants should carefully confirm: Whether their country is eligible. Whether their organization is an eligible applicant. Whether their project matches the specific call. Whether partnerships are required. Whether international partners are permitted. Whether co-financing is required. What expenses are eligible. The maximum available funding. The project duration. The exact application deadline. Required supporting documents. Evaluation criteria. These details can differ substantially between EU funding programmes and individual calls. Frequently Asked Questions What is Horizon Europe? Horizon Europe is the European Union s main research and innovation programme for 2021–2027 , with a budget of €95.5 billion . What does Horizon Europe fund? It supports research and innovation aimed at addressing global challenges, strengthening European competitiveness, supporting sustainable development, and creating and spreading excellent knowledge and technologies. Is Horizon Europe a scholarship? No. Horizon Europe is primarily a research and innovation funding programme , supporting projects and organizations rather than functioning as a conventional student scholarship. Is there one application deadline for Horizon Europe? No. Horizon Europe consists of numerous calls, each with its own eligibility requirements and deadlines. Can individuals apply? Eligibility depends on the specific call. Many EU research and innovation opportunities are structured around organizations, research institutions, companies, or collaborative consortia. Can organizations outside Europe participate? International participation can be possible in specific Horizon Europe calls, but eligibility varies. Applicants should check the individual call conditions rather than assuming worldwide eligibility. What is the EU4Health programme? EU4Health is the European Union s fourth and largest health programme since the launch of EU health programmes in 2003. It has a budget of €5.3 billion. What is the LIFE Programme? LIFE is an EU programme covering nature and biodiversity, circular economy and quality of life, climate change mitigation and adaptation, and clean energy transition. What is the Research Fund for Coal and Steel? RFCS supports research projects in the coal and steel sectors and can provide funding to universities, research centres, and private companies. Are all the programmes open to the same applicants? No. Each funding programme and individual call has its own eligibility conditions. Conclusion The European Commission s research and innovation funding ecosystem provides a broad range of opportunities for organizations working across research, technology, climate action, healthcare, environmental protection, regional development, sustainable energy, agriculture, and industrial innovation. At the centre of this ecosystem is Horizon Europe , the EU s €95.5 billion research and innovation programme for 2021–2027. Through Horizon Europe, the European Union seeks to support excellent research, technological development, international collaboration, climate action, the Sustainable Development Goals, economic growth, job creation, and European competitiveness. Beyond Horizon Europe, programmes such as EU4Health, LIFE, the European Regional Development Fund, the Cohesion Fund, the Technical Support Instrument, the European Structural and Investment Funds, and the Research Fund for Coal and Steel address additional priorities across health, climate, environment, regional development, economic cohesion, reform, agriculture, maritime activities, and industrial research. For researchers, universities, businesses, public institutions, and other eligible organizations, these programmes can provide important opportunities to secure funding for ambitious projects and turn innovative ideas into measurable social, environmental, scientific, and economic impact. However, there is no single deadline or universal eligibility requirement for all the programmes described on the page. Applicants must identify the specific funding call relevant to their project and carefully review its eligibility criteria, funding rules, partnership requirements, application procedure, and submission deadline before applying. title: U.S. Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029: Apply for a Two-Year Career in International Economic Policy
summary: The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship is now recruiting for its 2027–2029 cohort , offering a highly selective two-year opportunity for recent college graduates who want to contribute to international economic and financial policy in the United States. The Junior Fellowship places talented early-career professionals in the Treasury s Office of International Affairs (IA) , where they can gain direct exposure to international economic policy, financial developments, multilateral institutions, and high-level engagement with governments and international organizations. For graduates interested in international economics, public policy, finance, international relations, global development, financial diplomacy, or U.S. economic policy , this program offers an opportunity to begin a career at the center of U.S. international economic affairs. Junior Fellows may work on policy proposals, analyze international economic and financial developments, conduct analytical studies, and support senior Treasury officials participating in bilateral and multilateral meetings involving institutions and forums such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF), World Bank, G7, and G20 . The program is designed as a fixed two-year appointment, giving fellows an opportunity to develop specialized knowledge, professional experience, and a deeper understanding of how the U.S. government approaches international economic and financial issues. About the International Affairs Junior Fellowship The International Affairs Junior Fellowship is a highly selective early-career program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury s Office of International Affairs . It is designed specifically for new college graduates who want to work on issues affecting the international economy and the United States relationships with foreign governments and international financial institutions. During the two-year program, Junior Fellows can be exposed to multiple policy areas rather than being restricted to a single narrow subject. This allows participants to develop a broad understanding of: International economic policy Global financial developments International financial institutions Economic diplomacy Financial policy International trade Foreign exchange Export credits Regional economic relationships Multilateral cooperation U.S. engagement with international institutions The program can therefore provide a strong foundation for individuals considering long-term careers in government, international organizations, finance, policy research, consulting, academia, or related fields. What Junior Fellows Do Junior Fellows perform a variety of analytical, policy, and program-support responsibilities. Their work may include: Developing policy proposals Analyzing international economic developments Monitoring international financial developments Conducting analytical studies Supporting policy research Preparing materials for senior officials Supporting bilateral meetings Supporting multilateral meetings Participating in international policy discussions Developing knowledge of international economic and financial issues The fellowship is intended to provide meaningful exposure to the work of Treasury s Office of International Affairs rather than functioning simply as an observational placement. Exposure to International Economic Policy One of the most distinctive features of the program is the opportunity to work on issues affecting the international economic system. Junior Fellows may gain insight into how the U.S. government approaches economic relationships with countries and regions around the world. They can also develop an understanding of how international economic developments influence: U.S. economic policy Financial stability International trade Currency and foreign exchange issues Development finance Global economic cooperation International financial institutions This makes the program particularly relevant for graduates who want to understand the intersection of economics, diplomacy, finance, and government. Opportunities to Support IMF, World Bank, G7 and G20 Engagement Junior Fellows support bilateral and multilateral meetings involving senior Treasury officials and international counterparts. This can include engagement connected to major international institutions and forums such as: International Monetary Fund World Bank G7 G20 Junior Fellows often participate in these meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad. This exposure can provide valuable insight into how international economic policy is discussed and coordinated among governments and global institutions. Regional and Functional Office Placements Junior Fellows will be placed in either a regional office or a functional office within Treasury s Office of International Affairs. Regional Offices Regional offices oversee Treasury s engagement with counterpart finance ministries and treasuries around the world. Working in a regional office can provide fellows with exposure to the economic and financial relationships between the United States and specific countries or regions. Potential areas of learning include: Regional economic developments Bilateral economic relationships International financial policy Engagement with foreign finance ministries Economic and financial analysis Regional policy challenges Functional Offices Functional offices oversee Treasury s engagement with international financial institutions and help structure broader Treasury policy. Functional policy areas can include: International trade Export credits Foreign exchange International financial institutions Broader international economic policy The distinction between regional and functional offices allows fellows to develop expertise either around particular geographic relationships or around specialized international economic policy areas. Who Is the Fellowship Designed For? The program is intended for new college graduates and individuals who have recently completed, or are about to complete, their undergraduate education. Strong candidates will generally have a bachelor s degree with relevant academic preparation in areas such as: Economics Public policy Finance International relations Related disciplines The announcement specifically states that, because of the structure of the program, preference is given to undergraduates . Required Work and Extracurricular Experience In addition to academic qualifications, applicants must demonstrate 52 weeks, or 2,080 hours, of relevant experience . Importantly, the required experience does not have to come exclusively from traditional full-time employment. The announcement allows relevant experience to include: Paid employment Unpaid work Volunteer activities Extracurricular activities Work-study experiences Other relevant professional or academic activities Applicants should carefully document this experience in their resumes. The Junior Fellowship can serve as a launching point for a wide variety of professional and academic pathways. Career Development Opportunities During the fellowship, participants can develop skills that are valuable across government, business, academia, and international organizations. These may include: Economic analysis Financial analysis Policy research Policy writing International affairs analysis Government engagement Professional communication Meeting support Strategic thinking Research methodology Cross-cultural communication Multilateral policy engagement The experience can therefore provide a strong foundation for long-term careers in international economic affairs. Information Sessions for Applicants The Junior Fellows recruiting committee plans to host three information sessions before the application deadline. These sessions will be led by current fellows from various International Affairs offices. Frequently Asked Questions What is the International Affairs Junior Fellowship? It is a highly selective, fixed two-year program within the U.S. Department of the Treasury s Office of International Affairs for new college graduates interested in international economic policy. When is the application deadline? The application deadline is October 31, 2026 . When will selected fellows begin? Applications will be evaluated in December 2026, with fellows expected to begin in summer 2027 , or at another mutually agreed time. How long does the fellowship last? The program is a fixed two-year fellowship covering the 2027–2029 period. What degree is required? Strong candidates will have recently received, or will soon receive, a bachelor s degree with relevant coursework in economics, public policy, finance, international relations, or related fields. Is U.S. citizenship required? Yes. Applicants must confirm that they are U.S. citizens and must be able to provide documentation. Is professional experience required? Applicants must demonstrate 52 weeks or 2,080 hours of relevant paid or unpaid work, volunteer, or extracurricular experience. Can volunteer work count? Yes. The announcement specifically allows relevant volunteer and extracurricular experience to count toward the required experience. Can fellows travel internationally? Junior Fellows often participate in international meetings and may have opportunities to travel abroad . Is there a security clearance requirement? Yes. Candidates must be able to obtain and maintain a national security clearance . How many pages can the resume be? The resume should not exceed two pages . Is there an age limit? No specific age limit is stated in the provided announcement. The program is designed for new college graduates. Can international applicants apply? The program requires U.S. citizenship. Therefore, applicants who do not hold U.S. citizenship do not meet the stated eligibility requirement. Conclusion The U.S. Department of the Treasury International Affairs Junior Fellowship 2027–2029 offers an exceptional early-career pathway for qualified U.S. citizens who want to work at the intersection of international economics, finance, public policy, and global affairs. Through this highly selective two-year program, Junior Fellows can contribute to policy development, analyze international economic and financial developments, support senior Treasury officials, and gain exposure to major institutions and forums including the IMF, World Bank, G7, and G20. With opportunities to work in regional or functional offices, participate in international meetings, potentially travel abroad, and develop valuable analytical and policy skills, the fellowship can provide a strong foundation for careers in government, the private sector, international affairs, finance, and graduate education. Eligible recent or soon-to-be graduates should carefully prepare their cover letter, two-page resume, recommendation letter, transcripts, and required experience documentation before submitting their application to IAFellows@treasury.gov . The deadline is October 31, 2026 , making early preparation particularly important for candidates seeking to join the 2027–2029 International Affairs Junior Fellowship cohort.
